title: Teeny-Tiny
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A woman takes a bone from a graveyard; a tiny voice wants it back.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected and retold this tiny terror. A graveyard bone with an attitude—now that is a souvenir with backbone!
host.teaser: A little woman takes a little bone home from a graveyard. Then something starts asking for it back. Heh, even the smallest skeleton may have a bone to pick!
host.offerQuestion: Shall I dig up this tiny tale for you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Make yourself comfortable; I remember every word. I’ll tell it word for word, with nothing missing but a few of my teeth.
host.callback: That teeny-tiny voice from our tale certainly knew how to collect a debt. I admire the persistence; most of my bones stopped answering roll call years ago.
host.callbackShort: Our teeny-tiny visitor had a very particular bone to pick.

title: The Cauld Lad of Hilton
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Original includes an explicit aside about animal blood/sacrifice guarding treasure.
premise: A household brownie alternates between chores and pranks until the servants offer him clothing.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, an old patron and collector of tales, brought me this troublesome little house spirit. Housekeeping with a haunting included—what a grave improvement!
host.teaser: At Hilton Hall, a household spirit alternates between tidying the kitchen and wrecking it. The servants need a solution. I can sympathize; reliable help is murder to find.
host.offerQuestion: Care to meet this delightfully troublesome houseguest?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell Jacobs’s version word for word. My memory is beautifully preserved; the rest of me could use a better dusting.
host.callback: The Cauld Lad’s kitchen antics remain a delight to this old carcass. I respect anyone who makes the employment terms clear before the furniture starts flying.
host.callbackShort: That kitchen spirit made a hauntingly complicated employee.

title: The King o’ the Cats
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Cat death and a coffin, without gore.
premise: A man witnesses a cat funeral, then learns that his own cat knows more than expected.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected this feline funeral tale. Heh, tiny coffins and important cats—finally, a procession with some claws!
host.teaser: A sexton witnesses a funeral involving black cats, a tiny coffin, and a message for Tom. Back home, the household cat listens. Some family news arrives with a pallbearer.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we pay our respects to these mysterious cats?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Settle in for the exact words I remember. I’ll tell it word for word; a missing detail would be a grave discourtesy.
host.callback: That royal cat funeral still tickles my remaining ribs. Since telling you the tale, I’ve reserved a little extra dignity for the whiskered end of the guest list.
host.callbackShort: The King o’ the Cats made quite a grave impression.

title: An Uncomfortable Bed
author: Guy de Maupassant
premise: A guest at a country house becomes convinced that his prank-loving hosts have prepared a trick for him.

host.introduction: My old patron Guy de Maupassant brought me this bedroom mischief. Here is the old English telling; I’m already grinning through the gaps.
host.teaser: A houseguest suspects his prank-loving hosts have prepared a bedroom trap. He inspects the furniture and takes precautions. Ah, the elaborate things people do for a little peace and unrest!
host.offerQuestion: Would you like this little bedtime catastrophe?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Get comfortable; I remember this telling word for word. My own last bed had handles, but the story’s arrangements are rather more inventive.
host.callback: That suspicious houseguest gave bedtime a splendidly undignified turn. I still prefer a simple coffin; fewer opportunities to outwit the furniture and lose.
host.callbackShort: Our suspicious houseguest turned a night’s rest into an undertaking.

title: The Hedley Kow
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: An optimistic woman finds a treasure that keeps changing into something less valuable.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought this marvelously cheerful trickster story. It put a spring in my step—and one ankle on the floor.
host.teaser: An old woman finds a roadside treasure that refuses to stay the same thing. Her good cheer proves much harder to shift. A little supernatural mischief, with spirits remarkably high!
host.offerQuestion: Shall we follow this treasure through its peculiar changes?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you Jacobs’s telling word for word. The treasure may change, but these words are preserved better than my knees.
host.callback: That woman in the Hedley Kow tale kept her spirits up through every change of fortune. Admirable work; mine usually need a candle and a summoning circle.
host.callbackShort: The Hedley Kow could change the treasure, but not her spirits.

title: The Story of O-Tei
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Teenage betrothal and a dying adolescent’s self-devaluing beliefs about illness and marriage.
premise: A dying girl promises to return, and years later a traveler meets a familiar stranger.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn left me O-Tei’s story. A promise with prospects beyond the grave—he knew how to warm this chilly old heart.
host.teaser: A dying young woman promises that death need not end a betrothal. Years later, a traveler meets a strangely familiar woman at an inn. Some promises are terribly reluctant to lie down.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like a haunting with a little heart in it?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember every word of Hearn’s telling, and that is how I’ll share it. My memory keeps its promises, even when my joints don’t.
host.callback: O-Tei’s promise from our tale still warms the hollow beneath my ribs. There is something lovely about affection that refuses to read the expiry date.
host.callbackShort: O-Tei’s promise had no intention of staying buried.

title: The Open Window
author: Saki
advisories: A fabricated story of drowning and bereavement.
premise: A young hostess tells a nervous visitor why a window must remain open.

host.introduction: Saki was an old patron with a wickedly tidy delivery. He left this window open in my memory, and I’ve been cackling through the draught ever since.
host.teaser: A nervous visitor meets a young hostess beside an open window. She explains why it must stay open. Such a helpful child; I’m positively dying to hear her out.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we listen to the young hostess’s explanation?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Pull up a stool; I remember Saki’s words exactly. I’ll pass them on word for word, with my grin firmly attached for the occasion.
host.callback: Vera’s open-window tale remains a favorite beneath this decaying hairline. What marvelous economy: one window, a little conversation, and enough trouble to rattle a whole skeleton.
host.callbackShort: Vera knew how to give an open window grave significance.

title: Uncle Abraham’s Romance
author: E. Nesbit
premise: An elderly man recalls a young love he met in a churchyard at twilight.

host.introduction: My old patron E. Nesbit brought this churchyard romance to the bar. Love among the headstones—at last, a setting with room for my kind of charm.
host.teaser: An elderly man remembers meeting a young woman in a churchyard at twilight. A promise and the new moon draw them together. Romance does find the most delightfully quiet addresses.
host.offerQuestion: Care to linger over a little churchyard romance?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll share Nesbit’s telling word for word, as memory keeps it. Even a heart that has stopped can make room for a good story.
host.callback: Uncle Abraham’s twilight romance has kept its place beside my heart, or where my heart used to be. Some churchyard appointments deserve more tenderness than punctuality.
host.callbackShort: Uncle Abraham gave that churchyard a little life after dark.

title: The Golden Arm
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A greedy widower steals his dead wife’s golden arm and receives a midnight visitor.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected this greedy little graveyard tale. A golden arm, he said; I nearly offered a hand in exchange, but mine was depreciating.
host.teaser: A widower prizes his wife’s golden arm enough to take it from her grave. He brings his treasure home. Ah, inheritance can become such a hands-on business!
host.offerQuestion: Shall I lend you an earful of this golden-arm tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Jacobs’s telling word for word, and every word stays. We’ll leave the grave robbing to the story; I keep my memories intact.
host.callback: That golden-arm affair from our tale still gives my knuckles a happy rattle. A little ownership dispute becomes considerably livelier when the previous owner refuses to rest.
host.callbackShort: That golden arm came with a most persistent ownership claim.

title: The Shroud
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: A grieving mother is visited by her dead child, who asks her to let him rest.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm brought this tender haunting; Margaret Hunt gives us the English. I’ll lower my cackle for this one, dear guest.
host.teaser: A grieving mother sees her little boy return from the grave. He has something to tell her about her sorrow. A brief, tender haunting; even these old bones can keep quiet.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear this gentler ghost story?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember the telling exactly and will share it word for word. Let me tuck the jokes away; some visitors deserve a softer welcome.
host.callback: The little visitor in The Shroud remains tenderly lodged in my memory. Beneath all this excellent decay, I keep a soft spot for a ghost who needs kindness.
host.callbackShort: The Shroud gave these old bones a reason to quiet their rattling.

title: The Water-Nix
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: Two children flee a water spirit using ordinary objects that become magical obstacles.

host.introduction: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, my old patrons, supplied this watery escape; Margaret Hunt supplies the English. I love a tale that gets delightfully out of its depth.
host.teaser: Two children fall into a well and meet a water spirit with work for them. Escape may depend on a few ordinary objects. This employment arrangement sounds decidedly sink or swim.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we follow the children into this watery trouble?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you the remembered telling word for word. Not a word washed away; my memory is surprisingly watertight for something inside this skull.
host.callback: Those children in the Water-Nix tale certainly knew how to improvise an exit. I salute them with the arm that still bends; ordinary belongings can make extraordinary lifesavers.
host.callbackShort: The Water-Nix’s little employees refused to work themselves into an early grave.

title: The Strange Visitor
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A lonely woman wishes for company, and a visitor arrives one body part at a time.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought this visitor in pieces. Figuratively, that time; I do like the seating arrangements settled before the ankles arrive.
host.teaser: A lonely woman wishes for company by her fire. A visitor begins arriving, one body part at a time. Heh, some guests really do take an evening to pull themselves together!
host.offerQuestion: Shall we welcome this unusually assembled visitor?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember every piece of this telling and will give it word for word. Nothing missing; that is more than I can promise about my elbows.
host.callback: That strange visitor from our tale understood how to prolong an entrance. I love company, but I prefer knowing how many stools a collection of limbs will require.
host.callbackShort: Our strange visitor took making an entrance to pieces.

title: A Dead Secret
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Buddhist priest and burning a private letter.
Period gender assumptions about personal possessions.
premise: A woman’s ghost keeps returning to a drawer, and a priest searches for what troubles her.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn brought me this quiet haunting. A ghost with unfinished paperwork—now there is a soul who understands why the ledger never closes.
host.teaser: A woman’s ghost returns to the same room and watches a chest of drawers. Her family finds nothing; a priest looks more closely. Even the dead have private business to put in order.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to discover what troubles this quiet ghost?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll share Hearn’s telling word for word, just as I remember it. These memories stay properly filed, however untidy their keeper looks.
host.callback: O-Sono’s visits in A Dead Secret remain tucked carefully in my memory. I respect a private matter; a good host needn’t pry into every drawer that rattles.
host.callbackShort: O-Sono had unfinished business beyond the grave and inside a drawer.

title: Jorinda and Joringel
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: A witch traps young women as birds until a lover discovers a way to break the spell.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm brought this enchanted rescue; Margaret Hunt gives us the English. Such dangerous birdsong—music to my tattered ears!
host.teaser: Two lovers wander near a forest castle whose owner keeps a sinister collection of birds. One may soon join it. A pretty song can hide a very grave arrangement.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we venture near that castle and its cages?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember the telling word for word and will keep every word in place. No clipping its wings; I’m only here to open the cage.
host.callback: Jorinda and Joringel’s tale still gives these old ribs a hopeful flutter. A determined heart can be a formidable thing, even without a useful collection of sharp teeth.
host.callbackShort: Joringel’s rescue gave that witch’s household a wonderfully grave setback.

title: My Own Self
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Burn injury to a fairy child.
premise: A boy’s fireside playmate turns out to be a fairy, and a name trick saves him.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought this fireside mischief. Heh, introductions matter; I’ve spent ages deciding which name should go on my headstone.
host.teaser: A boy stays up beside the fire and meets a tiny playmate from the chimney. Their games grow dangerous. Before the evening ends, introductions may deserve rather more care than usual.
host.offerQuestion: Care to meet this small but troublesome fireside guest?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell Jacobs’s version word for word, as remembered. Every name remains exactly where it belongs; this skull is quite a respectable filing cabinet.
host.callback: That fireside game in My Own Self made excellent use of a careful introduction. I appreciate a good alias; there is plenty of room on a headstone for mistakes.
host.callbackShort: Our fireside tale made a very lively business of naming names.

title: The Old Witch
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: Two girls take service with a witch, but only one’s earlier kindness wins her help escaping.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected this witch’s tale. A dangerous employer and a difficult departure—enough to make even my long-dead feet itch for the road.
host.teaser: A girl helps strangers on her way to a new job, then finds herself working for a witch. Leaving may prove difficult. Some positions have positively dreadful severance terms.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to inspect this witch’s employment arrangements?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Jacobs’s telling exactly and will share it word for word. My memory never runs off the job, however tempting the exit looks.
host.callback: The road in The Old Witch remembered a kindness or two. That is the sort of loyalty I like to see; it puts a little spring in these cemetery feet.
host.callbackShort: That witch’s staffing problem became a splendid escape story.

title: Kate Crackernuts
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Head transformed into a sheep’s head.
a bird is killed for a cure.
premise: A resourceful young woman enters a fairy hill to help an enchanted sister and a sick prince.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected Kate Crackernuts and brought her midnight business to my bar. Secret excursions! I almost rattled myself apart asking for the particulars.
host.teaser: Kate has an enchanted sister to help and a prince whose secret nightly trips leave him ill. She follows the clues. A sensible head is useful when everyone else is losing theirs.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we join Kate on her midnight investigation?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Every word is waiting in my memory, and every word will reach you unchanged. Kate keeps track of clues; I keep track of tales and occasionally my fingers.
host.callback: Kate Crackernuts remains excellent company in my memory. I admire a guest who follows the details instead of falling to pieces; my own record there is rather patchy.
host.callbackShort: Kate kept her wits while the midnight mysteries piled up.

title: Mujina
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Brief discussion of possible suicide; no graphic self-harm.
premise: A man stops to help a weeping stranger on a dark road and sees something impossible.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn left Mujina with me after dark. A lonely road and uncertain company—enough to put a delighted clatter in my teeth.
host.teaser: A traveler stops to help a weeping woman beside a lonely road. Something about the encounter sends him seeking a distant lantern. Ah, reassurance looks so inviting from a distance.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we follow that lantern into a little trouble?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell Hearn’s tale word for word; my memory has kept its face. Much more faithfully than some of my other features, I’m pleased to report.
host.callback: Mujina’s lonely road still brightens the dark corners of my skull. What a marvelous tale of appearances; I give my own face a quick inventory whenever I recall it.
host.callbackShort: Mujina made putting on a friendly face rather complicated.

title: Oshidori
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Animal death and graphic self-inflicted death.
premise: A hunter kills one of a pair of ducks and receives a grieving visit in his dreams.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn brought this sorrowful haunting. It has real feeling beneath the feathers; even a merry old corpse knows when to lower his voice.
host.teaser: A hunter kills a duck and dreams of a grieving woman asking him to return to the water. This brief haunting carries sorrow and a cruel image; the grave casts a long shadow.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like this brief, sorrowful tale by the water?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Hearn’s words exactly, and I’ll give them to you unchanged. I’ll keep my cackle quiet; this haunting has its own voice.
host.callback: The sorrow in Oshidori remains with the story I told you. I keep it gently; even a heart as thoroughly retired as mine can make room for grief.
host.callbackShort: Oshidori leaves my cheerful old bones a little quieter.

title: Mr. Miacca
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Threatened child cannibalism and apparent amputation, revealed to involve furniture.
premise: A boy captured by a hungry bogeyman survives by persuading and tricking his captors.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected this hungry little horror. Mr. Miacca has dreadful dining manners; I nearly laughed a molar into the cutlery drawer.
host.teaser: A wandering boy ends up in Mr. Miacca’s home, where supper is under discussion. Unfortunately, the invitation is rather personal. Quick thinking may be the most useful thing on the menu.
host.offerQuestion: Care to hear about this alarmingly hungry host?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll serve Jacobs’s telling word for word, exactly as I remember it. No trimming; I keep that sort of cutlery well away from a guest’s story.
host.callback: Mr. Miacca’s supper plans still give my ribs a merry shake. The tale makes a strong case for quick wits and hosts who keep their guests off the menu.
host.callbackShort: Mr. Miacca’s intended supper proved delightfully unwilling to cooperate.

title: The Singing Bone
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Fratricide, violent boar, skeleton, execution by drowning.
premise: A murdered man’s bone becomes a musical instrument that tells the truth about his death.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm brought this musical bone; Margaret Hunt gives us the English. Finally, an instrument I might have a spare part for!
host.teaser: Two brothers face a dangerous beast, but courage isn’t their only difficulty. Years later, a shepherd finds a most unusual bone. Some relics are simply dying for an audience.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear what this remarkable bone has to say?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember the telling word for word and will repeat it faithfully. Every bone in this story stays accounted for; mine should take the hint.
host.callback: That singing bone from our tale still sets my toes tapping, when I can find them. What a splendid witness: very little flesh, and plenty to say.
host.callbackShort: The singing bone gave buried business a public performance.

title: Binnorie
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Sibling murder, drowning, bones and hair made into an instrument.
premise: A murdered princess’s remains become a harp that exposes the person who drowned her.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought Binnorie to the bar. A harp with grave matters on its mind—just my sort of entertainment!
host.teaser: Two sisters go to a millstream, and only one returns. Later, a harper finds material for an extraordinary instrument. Its music promises more than a pleasant evening’s rattling.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear this harp’s unsettling business?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll share Jacobs’s telling word for word, as memory preserves it. Every note accounted for; I do hate leaving a good tale dismembered.
host.callback: Binnorie’s harp still has an honored place in this crumbling skull. A wonderful performer; it brings its own story and refuses to let the room bury the subject.
host.callbackShort: Binnorie’s harp made an unforgettable case for listening to the dead.

title: Fairy Ointment
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A nurse tries a magical ointment and sees the hidden world of the fairies.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected this tale of fairy ointment. It opened my eyes; rather an achievement, considering what the years have done to the lids.
host.teaser: A nurse is summoned at midnight to care for a stranger’s baby. An unusual ointment reveals what her hosts would rather conceal. An eye-opening appointment, with something sinister behind the welcome.
host.offerQuestion: Care to peek behind these fairies’ carefully kept appearances?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Jacobs’s telling word for word and will pass it on intact. No cosmetic improvements; I know when to leave a well-preserved thing alone.
host.callback: Dame Goody’s fairy ointment remains a memorable appointment from our tales. I admire discretion in a guest; some hosts are much less forgiving than this cheerful old ruin.
host.callbackShort: Dame Goody found that seeing everything can carry a dreadful price.

title: The Master and His Pupil
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Explicit demon summoning, ritual magic, supernatural threat.
premise: An apprentice opens a forbidden book and summons a being he cannot control.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, an old patron and collector of tales, brought this forbidden-book business. I cackled until my jaw slipped; some assistants take instructions far too seriously.
host.teaser: A pupil is left alone with his master’s forbidden book. Reading aloud brings an alarming visitor who expects instructions. An excellent lesson in checking the terms before raising the help.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we open this troublesome little book?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you Jacobs’s words exactly as I remember them. The telling stays word for word; I leave unauthorized alterations to the apprentice.
host.callback: That master and pupil still amuse the dust beneath my scalp. A little knowledge can summon quite a staffing problem, especially when the help won’t take a hint.
host.callbackShort: That pupil raised help before considering how to dismiss it.

title: Shadow—A Parable
author: Edgar Allan Poe
advisories: Biblical epigraph and classical religious imagery.
premise: At a plague-time gathering, a shadow unlike any ordinary shadow appears among the mourners.

host.introduction: My old patron Edgar Allan Poe brought this shadow to the bar. Heh, an uninvited presence at a gathering—at least it keeps the atmosphere from going dead.
host.teaser: During a pestilence, seven people gather behind a sealed bronze door. Wine and lamplight offer poor defenses against a shadow that belongs to none of them. The guest list may need another line.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we join this gathering and its unexpected shadow?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I remember Poe’s telling word for word, and I’ll keep it so. No shadow of a doubt in this old skull; the shadows are all in the tale.
host.callback: That shadow at Poe’s gathering remains excellent company in my memory. What an entrance: no knocking, no introduction, and every eye in the room suddenly interested.
host.callbackShort: Poe’s shadow knew how to bring grave matters to the table.

title: Tamlane
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Tithe to the Fiend/netherworld, holy-water circle and Christian ritual, threatened mutilation.
Brief nonsexual nudity during magical transformation.
premise: On Halloween, Janet must hold her enchanted lover through frightening transformations to rescue him.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected this Halloween rescue. Lovers, fairies, and alarming transformations—enough to make a decrepit bartender feel quite festive!
host.teaser: On Halloween, Janet has one chance to rescue her lover from the fairy court. She must recognize him and hold fast through frightening changes. A romantic attachment with some grave complications!
host.offerQuestion: Shall we join Janet for this dangerous Halloween appointment?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Jacobs’s telling word for word and will hold fast to every word. These fingers may loosen, but my grip on a story never does.
host.callback: Janet’s Halloween rescue in Tamlane still puts life in this old husk. That is what I call holding a relationship together; my own elbows could learn a thing or two.
host.callbackShort: Janet gave holding on for dear life a splendid Halloween demonstration.

title: The Golden Ball
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Threatened execution, giants cut in half, severed limbs.
premise: A young man spends three nights in a monster-filled house to save his sweetheart from hanging.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought me these dreadful lodgings. Three nights in a monster-filled house—finally, somewhere my snoring wouldn’t cause complaints!
host.teaser: A young woman faces terrible danger after losing a golden ball. Her sweetheart seeks it in a strange house with monstrous residents. Recovery promises to be a thoroughly grave undertaking.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to inspect these alarmingly occupied lodgings?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll recount Jacobs’s tale word for word, exactly as remembered. Three nights of trouble kept fresh; no embalming required for a story this lively.
host.callback: That search for the golden ball still rattles pleasantly around my skull. Three nights with those residents would make even a drafty coffin look like a thoughtful accommodation.
host.callbackShort: The golden-ball search made lodging with monsters a serious undertaking.

title: The Three Army-Surgeons
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Self-amputation, removed eyes/heart, stolen corpse parts, animal organs.
premise: Traveling surgeons remove their own organs, but an overnight mishap gives them strange replacements.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm supplied these surgeons; Margaret Hunt gives us the English. Spare parts and lodging mishaps—at last, something with practical interest for me!
host.teaser: Three surgeons demonstrate their remarkable skills at an inn, leaving some vital belongings in another person’s care. Morning promises complications. A truly hands-on introduction to the lost-property department!
host.offerQuestion: Shall we check in on these wonderfully reckless surgeons?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember the telling word for word, and every part will reach you intact. That is a service guarantee these surgeons might have appreciated.
host.callback: Those army-surgeons from our tale still make me cackle into my collar. I keep a closer watch on my own spare parts; replacements can have such unexpected personalities.
host.callbackShort: Those surgeons made checking out of an inn an anatomical challenge.

title: A Diagnosis of Death
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: A man tells his doctor about an ominous figure he saw in a rented house.

host.introduction: My old patron Ambrose Bierce brought this medical mystery to the bar. A dreadful visitor and a diagnosis—he certainly knew how to cheer up a walking corpse.
host.teaser: A man tells his physician about a disturbing figure seen in a rented house. Reasonable explanations are available. The difficulty is what that visitor appeared to know; a rather grave detail.
host.offerQuestion: Care to sit in on this unsettling consultation?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I’ll share Bierce’s telling word for word; I remember it perfectly. My medical chart may be alarming, but the memory remains in excellent working order.
host.callback: A Diagnosis of Death remains a favorite in my crumbling case notes. Bierce packed so much trouble into one visit; I do admire an efficient bedside menace.
host.callbackShort: Bierce’s diagnosis gave that visitor a distinctly grave significance.

title: Godfather Death
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: A physician gains the power to know who will die, then tries to outwit Death.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm brought this physician’s bargain; Margaret Hunt supplies the English. Death as a godfather—now there is someone who remembers the family appointments!
host.teaser: A physician’s supernatural patron can tell which patients will recover and which will die. Fame follows, then temptation. Success has a dreadful habit of making the fine print seem optional.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to meet this remarkably punctual godfather?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember this telling word for word and will keep its terms exactly. Death may audit the candles; I audit the syllables.
host.callback: Godfather Death’s candles still burn clearly in my memory. That physician certainly had a memorable sponsor; I prefer family favors with fewer opportunities for a final account.
host.callbackShort: Godfather Death kept a very grave eye on the candlelight.

title: The Oval Portrait
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A wounded traveler discovers a portrait in a remote château that seems impossibly alive.

host.introduction: My old patron Edgar Allan Poe brought me this portrait’s story. Such devotion to preserving appearances! I felt almost envious, then remembered what happened to my own complexion.
host.teaser: A wounded traveler shelters in a château and finds a portrait that seems impossibly alive. A little book records its history. This picture may be worth rather more than a thousand shudders.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we take a closer look at that portrait?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I’ll give you Poe’s telling word for word, exactly as it stays in my memory. No touch-ups; I know when a portrait should be left alone.
host.callback: Poe’s oval portrait remains vividly framed inside this dusty skull. What a dreadful commission; even I prefer my art to keep a little distance from the business of preservation.
host.callbackShort: That oval portrait gave lifelike art a most unsettling definition.

title: The Pied Piper of Franchville
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Mass rat drowning and disappearance of children.
premise: A town refuses to pay its mysterious ratcatcher, who returns with a different tune.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought Franchville’s piper to my attention. Music and an unpaid bill—ah, the rhythm of a grave misunderstanding!
host.teaser: A rat-plagued town hires a mysterious piper, who does exactly as promised. Then payment becomes a question. I do hope they appreciate a performer with such a lively command of the room.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear about Franchville’s musical arrangement?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Jacobs’s telling word for word, and not a word is shortchanged. My memory keeps a straighter ledger than certain townsfolk.
host.callback: Franchville’s piper still has an honored entry in my memory. That tale gives an unsettled bill such dreadful resonance; enough to make the coins rattle with my bones.
host.callbackShort: Franchville discovered that a tune can carry a very grave account.

title: The Voice of Death
author: Traditional Romanian tale; in Andrew Lang (editor)
advisories: Implied mass deaths and a fatal abyss.
premise: A man searches for a country without death, where people follow a mysterious voice and vanish.

host.introduction: My old patron Andrew Lang brought this traditional Romanian tale from the collection he edited. A country without death! I nearly choked on the dust in my throat.
host.teaser: A wealthy man seeks a country where nobody dies and believes he has found it. Residents sometimes follow a mysterious voice and never return. A little custom worth examining before settling down.
host.offerQuestion: Care to visit this suspiciously deathless country?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll share this English telling word for word, exactly as I remember it. My memory never answers mysterious invitations to disappear.
host.callback: That country in The Voice of Death remains a marvel of reassuring language. I still admire the salesmanship, with one eyebrow raised as high as the stitches permit.
host.callbackShort: That deathless country had some decidedly grave terms of residence.

title: Frau Trude
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Child transformed into firewood and burned.
premise: A curious girl visits a forbidden house and discovers the true nature of its resident.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm brought Frau Trude; Margaret Hunt supplies the English. Such a short visit, such dreadful hospitality—I’m positively rattling to tell it.
host.teaser: A curious girl is forbidden to visit Frau Trude’s strange house. Naturally, the warning makes the doorway more tempting. A very brief, very dark appointment awaits inside.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I tell you about this dreadfully unwelcoming house?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember every word and will give the telling unchanged. A tiny tale, carefully preserved; some horrors take very little shelf space.
host.callback: Frau Trude’s house remains off my list of hospitable establishments. I may be a grinning corpse, but I have very firm opinions about treating a guest properly.
host.callbackShort: Frau Trude gave a short visit a dreadfully final feeling.

title: John Mortonson's Funeral
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: An impeccably arranged funeral is interrupted by a dreadful discovery inside the coffin.

host.introduction: My old patron Ambrose Bierce brought me John Mortonson’s funeral. Such solemn arrangements, such grisly possibilities—he knew exactly how to tickle the ribs I had left.
host.teaser: John Mortonson’s funeral proceeds with dignity, quiet mourners, and everything properly arranged. Then comes an interruption. A very short, grisly tale; solemnity can be such a fragile lid on a coffin.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like this brief and grisly funeral surprise?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I remember Bierce’s telling word for word and will deliver every word. No rearranging the remains; the original arrangement is dreadful enough.
host.callback: John Mortonson’s funeral still produces an undignified rattle in my chest. Bierce could overturn an entire room’s composure without giving the mourners time to straighten their collars.
host.callbackShort: That funeral gave solemn proceedings a horribly lively interruption.

title: The Hobyahs
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Repeated mutilation and death of a pet dog, cannibalism, kidnapped child.
premise: Night creatures stalk a fragile house while its owners silence the dog that warns them.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected the Hobyahs and brought their nighttime business to the bar. A barking dog has my attention; these ears are falling apart, not closed.
host.teaser: Creatures visit a fragile little house after dark, and the dog keeps sounding the alarm. The household wants sleep. Being dead tired is understandable; ignoring a warning is another matter.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear what has that little dog so alarmed?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll tell Jacobs’s version word for word, exactly as I remember it. No silencing the warnings; I have excellent hearing for a man with these ears.
host.callback: The Hobyahs remain a particularly dreadful set of nighttime callers. Since that tale, I give a barking dog full professional courtesy; a useful warning deserves more than a tired groan.
host.callbackShort: The Hobyahs made that dog’s alarm a matter of grave importance.

title: Staley Fleming’s Hallucination
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: A patient asks a physician for help with an animal that appears at his bedside each night.

host.introduction: My old patron Ambrose Bierce brought Staley Fleming’s bedside trouble to my bar. A threatening nightly visitor—just the sort of appointment that makes my teeth chatter with anticipation.
host.teaser: A man asks his doctor about a threatening dog that appears beside his bed each night. Questions invite a troubling explanation. Some bedside company is dreadfully difficult to dismiss.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear about this persistent bedside visitor?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I’ll share Bierce’s tale word for word, exactly as I remember it. These memories stay put; I’ve never needed to chain one to the bedpost.
host.callback: Staley Fleming’s nightly visitor still prowls through my excellent memory. A delightfully dreadful consultation; reassuring words can sound rather thin when trouble comes equipped with teeth.
host.callbackShort: Staley Fleming’s bedside problem gave reassurance something to chew on.

title: Mr. Fox
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Murdered women, severed hand, violent revenge. Related to The Robber Bridegroom.
premise: A bride-to-be enters her suitor’s secluded home and discovers why she should fear him.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought me Lady Mary’s inquiry. A charming suitor with a secluded house—heh, such promising grounds for grave suspicion!
host.teaser: Lady Mary investigates her charming suitor’s secluded house. Warnings above its doorways grow increasingly peculiar. Good manners are lovely, but they make dreadfully thin protection against what waits farther inside.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we follow Lady Mary through those unsettling doorways?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Jacobs’s telling word for word and will repeat it faithfully. Every warning stays visible; I never bury useful information beneath the bar.
host.callback: Lady Mary’s visit to Mr. Fox remains a splendid investigation in my memory. I admire a guest who reads the warnings before deciding where to hang a coat—or anything else.
host.callbackShort: Mr. Fox’s doorways put some grave qualifications on his charm.

title: The Rose-Tree
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Child beheading, family cannibalism, abusive stepmother, fatal crushing. Variant of The Juniper-Tree.
premise: A murdered child returns as a singing bird that brings gifts and a terrible reckoning.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected this rose-tree tale. Such a lovely song rooted in such dreadful business; it nearly shook the grave dust from my sleeves.
host.teaser: A child disappears, a family meal conceals something dreadful, and a bird begins to sing. This is a harsh old tale. Beautiful music can have the most appalling family background.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like this dark tale of the rose-tree’s song?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you Jacobs’s telling word for word; my memory has kept every word. No pruning the tale, however dreadful its branches become.
host.callback: The rose-tree’s bird still sings clearly in my dusty memory. What a performer; it gives buried family business the sort of airing no polite gathering can ignore.
host.callbackShort: The rose-tree’s song brought dreadful family business out of the ground.

title: The Mystery of the Semi-Detached
author: E. Nesbit
premise: A young man waiting for his sweetheart sees something impossible inside her house.

host.introduction: My old patron E. Nesbit brought this little property mystery to the bar. A desirable address with dreadful prospects—enough to make a coffin seem an uncomplicated purchase.
host.teaser: A young man visits his sweetheart’s house and sees something impossible inside. Ordinary rooms suddenly hold a terrible question. This brief tale carries a violent image and a distinctly unhealthy atmosphere.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we take this brief, unsettling look inside?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I remember Nesbit’s telling word for word and will leave every word in place. My memory keeps its tenants longer than any respectable lease allows.
host.callback: That glimpse inside the semi-detached house still occupies a corner of my skull. Nesbit made domestic arrangements wonderfully dreadful; I’m content with a bar and a modest burial plot.
host.callbackShort: That semi-detached house had a grave problem with its view.

title: The Lady and the Ghost
author: Rose Cecil O’Neill
premise: A fashionable woman receives a visit from a ghost whose romantic assumptions disappoint her.

host.introduction: My old patron Rose Cecil O’Neill brought me this fashionable haunting. A romantic entrance from beyond the grave—oh, I do love a fellow corpse with social ambitions!
host.teaser: A fashionable lady receives a ghost with romantic expectations. Returning from the grave is one difficulty; managing the conversation may be another. Some courtships begin with an awfully dead silence.
host.offerQuestion: Care for a little romance with these socially troubled spirits?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I’ll share O’Neill’s own words, exactly as I remember them. Every awkward pause preserved; this old carcass appreciates a beautifully executed entrance.
host.callback: That lady and her ambitious ghost still amuse the dust behind my eyes. Returning from the grave is quite an achievement; finding the right thing to say remains a separate undertaking.
host.callbackShort: That ghost’s romantic hopes met a wonderfully awkward reception.

title: Little Red-Cap
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: wolf cut open, filled with stones.
premise: A girl’s woodland visit to her grandmother becomes an encounter with a deceptive wolf.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm brought this woodland visit; Margaret Hunt supplies the English. Such interest in grandmother’s teeth—I felt quite self-conscious about my remaining three.
host.teaser: A girl takes a basket to her grandmother and meets a wolf with unusually helpful questions. The woodland path looks innocent enough. Heh, appearances can have rather excellent teeth.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we join Little Red-Cap on that woodland visit?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember this English telling word for word, and every word stays. No filing down the teeth; I preserve a tale’s original bite.
host.callback: Little Red-Cap’s visit still gives my remaining teeth a cheerful chatter. That woodland tale makes a remarkable case for looking closely at anyone claiming to be the family.
host.callbackShort: Little Red-Cap’s family visit came with unusually grave dental concerns.

title: The Wolves of Cernogratz
author: Saki
premise: At an old castle, a servant contradicts the owners’ explanation of a family legend.

host.introduction: Saki, my old patron, brought Cernogratz and its wolves to the bar. A family legend with a howl in it—music to these delightfully decomposing ears!
host.teaser: At an old castle, the owners explain the legend behind the wolves’ howling. An elderly servant remembers differently. A house may change hands while its history keeps a much firmer grip.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear what those wolves might remember?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll give you Saki’s telling word for word, just as memory keeps it. Old histories deserve care; I’ve had several centuries of practice looking after remains.
host.callback: The wolves of Cernogratz still have their place in my memory. I admire a family history that refuses to stay quietly buried merely because the furniture has changed owners.
host.callbackShort: Cernogratz’s wolves kept the family history from resting quietly.

title: Tom Tit Tot
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Repeated threats of execution by a husband.
premise: A desperate young woman bargains with a strange spinner whose hidden name could save her.

host.introduction: My old patron Joseph Jacobs collected Tom Tit Tot and brought its bargain here. Impossible work and a secret name—now there is a contract worth reading before your eyes rot.
host.teaser: A young woman must spin impossible quantities of flax or face a king’s fury. A strange little helper offers terms. A hidden name may matter more than any thread she can produce.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we examine this little spinner’s dangerous bargain?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Jacobs’s telling word for word and will keep every syllable. Especially the names; even a dusty skull knows where the important bones belong.
host.callback: Tom Tit Tot’s secret still tickles this old ruin of a face. That tale shows how a few well-chosen words can give a dreadful bargain an unexpectedly lively turn.
host.callbackShort: That little spinner made a grave mistake about keeping his name private.

title: The Spirit in the Bottle
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
premise: A student uncorks a bottle in the woods and must outwit the giant spirit he releases.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm brought this bottled spirit; Margaret Hunt gives us the English. I love good glassware, especially when the contents have dreadful manners!
host.teaser: A woodcutter’s son finds a sealed bottle beneath an old tree. The voice inside wants freedom. Uncorking a spirit can be a grave undertaking when it has opinions about the service.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear what is rattling inside that bottle?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I’ll give you the telling word for word, exactly as I remember it. No spilling the details; I’ve kept this particular spirit very carefully bottled.
host.callback: That spirit in the bottle remains a splendid example of poor guest manners. I enjoy its tale enormously; a sound stopper can be such a comforting piece of equipment.
host.callbackShort: Our bottled spirit needed a grave lesson in thanking its host.

title: The Buried Moon
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Drowning danger, threatening dead things/bogles, Christian protective signs and charms.
premise: The Moon is trapped by marsh creatures, leaving villagers to venture into darkness to rescue her.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought me the buried Moon. Imagine misplacing that much light; I can barely keep track of one wandering kneecap!
host.teaser: The Moon ventures into a marsh to investigate its creatures. Then the nights stay dark, and villagers must search for their missing light. Something dreadful has put the evening under a shroud.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we look for the Moon in that troublesome marsh?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Jacobs’s telling word for word and will pass it on unchanged. These memories glow nicely, despite the considerable dust inside their keeper.
host.callback: The rescue of the buried Moon still lights a corner of this old skull. I’m fond of a tale where courage gives the darkness something to be nervous about.
host.callbackShort: Those villagers refused to let the Moon remain under a shroud.

title: The She-Wolf
author: Saki
premise: A boast about supernatural powers becomes the basis of a country-house surprise.

host.introduction: My old patron Saki brought this house-party business to my bar. Boasts of supernatural power! I nearly laughed my jaw loose waiting for someone to request a demonstration.
host.teaser: A guest claims unusual powers, and his hostess asks to become a wolf. The party grows interested in a demonstration. Some drawing rooms are positively dying for a little less polite conversation.
host.offerQuestion: Care to hear about this house party’s hairy complications?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll share Saki’s telling word for word, exactly as I remember it. No transformation of the text; that entertaining business belongs to the house party.
host.callback: That she-wolf affair remains wonderful entertainment in my memory. Saki could put fangs into a drawing-room conversation without so much as troubling his collar; an admirable talent.
host.callbackShort: The she-wolf gave that party’s conversation a delightfully alarming bite.

title: A Jug of Sirup
author: Ambrose Bierce
advisories: brief references to Salem witchcraft accusations.
premise: A village merchant appears to keep serving customers after everyone has attended his funeral.

host.introduction: My old patron Ambrose Bierce brought me Silas Deemer’s business arrangements. A shopkeeper who won’t let death interrupt the service—at last, someone who understands my work ethic!
host.teaser: Silas Deemer has died, yet a customer receives service at his supposedly empty shop. The neighbors investigate. Keeping late hours is one thing; keeping the proprietor late is rather more intriguing.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we visit this remarkably persistent shopkeeper?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I remember Bierce’s tale word for word and will give you the full telling. The stock stays fresh, even when the shopkeeper is considerably past his date.
host.callback: Silas Deemer’s shop still earns my professional admiration. That tale understands a host’s attachment to the place; some of us simply refuse to let a funeral spoil the opening hours.
host.callbackShort: Silas Deemer gave late service an impressively literal meaning.

title: An Inhabitant of Carcosa
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: A traveler searches a desolate landscape for his home and encounters signs that time is out of joint.

host.introduction: My old patron Ambrose Bierce brought Carcosa into this bar one evening. Such desolation! I felt a cheerful little draught blow straight through the vacancy behind my ribs.
host.teaser: A traveler searches a desolate landscape for his familiar city. Strange stones and an unfamiliar sky offer little help. The place seems to have buried its directions along with several other important details.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to wander a little way toward Carcosa?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I’ll tell Bierce’s words exactly as I remember them. Nothing lost from the telling; I keep a better map of my memories than of my scattered joints.
host.callback: Carcosa’s lonely landscape remains wonderfully clear inside my skull. A dreadful place to misplace one’s bearings; I’m glad to have you here where a familiar bar can offer company.
host.callbackShort: Carcosa made finding home a matter of grave uncertainty.

title: The Lambton Worm
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
advisories: Bloody combat, dog beheading, threatened killing of a parent.
premise: A discarded creature grows into a monstrous serpent, and killing it demands a dangerous vow.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought the Lambton Worm to my attention. A fishing story with monstrous prospects—now that is something to sink my remaining teeth into!
host.teaser: A young man discards a strange catch, which grows into a menace while he is away. Facing it demands unusual armor and a troubling promise. An afternoon’s fishing can leave a dreadful inheritance.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear how that fishing trip grew teeth?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I remember Jacobs’s telling word for word and will pass on every word. No exaggerating the catch; this old tale has quite enough backbone of its own.
host.callback: The Lambton Worm still curls comfortably through my memory. What a magnificent warning about unfinished business; leave something troublesome behind, and it may grow into a very grave appointment.
host.callbackShort: That Lambton fishing trip left an awfully lively problem behind.

title: Yuki-Onna
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Death by freezing, threat to kill a spouse, family separation.
premise: A woodcutter survives an encounter with a snow spirit by promising never to speak of it.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn brought this winter tale. Heh, even my marrow asked for a blanket.
host.teaser: Two woodcutters shelter from a blizzard when a woman in white appears. One survives by promising silence. A secret can keep a person warm, until it starts giving them the chills.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I unearth this little winter secret for you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Get comfortable; I remember every frozen syllable. I'll tell it word for word, with nothing lost to frostbite.
host.callback: That was Yuki-Onna's winter secret I shared with you. I admire a tale that can chill the bones without borrowing the ice bucket.
host.callbackShort: Yuki-Onna made secrecy a matter of grave importance. Heh!

title: Of a Mirror and a Bell
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Suicide, shame, ritual cursing and straw effigy.
premise: A donated mirror resists melting into a temple bell, beginning a chain of strange promises and curses.

host.introduction: Lafcadio Hearn, an old patron of mine, brought a tale of a troublesome bell. I positively rattled with delight; finally, competition for my knees.
host.teaser: A woman donates her treasured mirror to a temple bell, but the mirror refuses to melt. Regret, strange promises, and ringing metal follow. Some gifts arrive with grave strings attached.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I ring in this deliciously troublesome tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I'll repeat it word for word from memory. Every clang is preserved; my hearing has survived rather better than my ears.
host.callback: I remember sharing the mirror and the bell with you. What a commotion over one reluctant donation; enough to wake the neighborhood cemetery.
host.callbackShort: That mirror-and-bell business still tickles my funny bone with every clang.

title: The Hollow of the Three Hills
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
premise: A desperate woman asks an old crone to let her hear what has become of the people she left behind.

host.introduction: Nathaniel Hawthorne, an old bar patron, brought me these three hills. Metaphorically, of course; I only have room for one burial mound behind the bottles.
host.teaser: In a lonely hollow, a desperate woman asks an old crone for news of those she left behind. The answers arrive as unsettling sounds. This magic has a distinctly cold bedside manner.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to descend into this mournful little hollow?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Settle beside me; I'll recall it word for word. These voices are better preserved than the rest of my collection of bones.
host.callback: Hawthorne's three hills were our destination in that tale. Such a small hollow for so much sorrow; I keep a warm welcome ready afterward.
host.callbackShort: Those three hills concealed a grave little conversation.

title: Childe Rowland
author: Joseph Jacobs (collector and reteller)
premise: A young man enters Elfland’s Dark Tower to recover his missing sister and brothers.

host.introduction: Joseph Jacobs, my old patron and collector of tales, brought his telling of Childe Rowland. Rules, towers, missing relatives; a family outing with real backbone!
host.teaser: A vanished sister draws her brothers toward Elfland's Dark Tower. The youngest carries two vital rules into the enchanted country. I do love directions that might keep a fellow in one piece.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we give Elfland's dark little doorway a knock?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I'll tell Jacobs's version word for word. My memory keeps every rule; pity it can't keep all my teeth.
host.callback: Childe Rowland's journey was the tale I shared with you. Elfland puts a wonderfully sinister spin on reading the instructions before dinner.
host.callbackShort: Childe Rowland's rules were worth keeping close to the rib cage.

title: The Outsider
author: H. P. Lovecraft
premise: An isolated resident of a dark castle climbs toward light and the hope of meeting other people.

host.introduction: My old patron H. P. Lovecraft brought me a lonely castle dweller. A guest craving company! That always gets the little scrap of heart I have left beating.
host.teaser: A solitary figure climbs out of a dark castle, hoping to find light and company. Beyond those walls waits an unfamiliar world. Even a gloomy old ghoul can appreciate wanting an invitation.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we follow this lonely soul toward the light?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Make yourself welcome; I'll remember it word for word. No passage has crumbled, though a few of my joints have.
host.callback: I shared the Outsider's search for company with you. There is always room at my bar for a lonely soul; mine has been rattling around here for ages.
host.callbackShort: The Outsider wanted company. That longing goes straight through my ribs.

title: Fitcher’s Bird
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Abducted women, chopped bodies, reassembly/resurrection, skull, perpetrators burned alive.
premise: A woman taken by a murderous wizard uses disguise and ingenuity to rescue her sisters.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm supplied this tale, in Margaret Hunt's English. A wizard with a forbidden room; that always opens my coffin lid a little.
host.teaser: A wizard gives his captive keys to a splendid house, forbids one room, and entrusts her with a little object. His rules leave precious little room for mistakes. Heh, some hosts have truly rotten manners.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like a peek at this wizard's dreadful house rules?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I'll recall Margaret Hunt's English word for word. Every piece stays in place; an arrangement my own skeleton could learn from.
host.callback: That was Fitcher's Bird I told you. Such inventiveness in a dreadful house; I still give the clever visitor a round of bony applause.
host.callbackShort: Fitcher's Bird still deserves a rattle of applause from these old bones.

title: The Robber Bridegroom
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Cannibalism, murder and dismemberment of a woman, severed finger. Related to Mr. Fox.
premise: A young woman visits her intended husband’s forest house and witnesses a horrifying crime.

host.introduction: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, old patrons both, brought this forest bridegroom; Margaret Hunt supplies the English. I've heard wedding bells with less of a funeral undertone.
host.teaser: A young woman follows a forest trail to her future husband's house. Its welcome feels terribly wrong, and leaving may take considerable care. Courtship can have some appalling skeletons in its closet.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I introduce this deeply unsuitable bridegroom?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Here comes Margaret Hunt's English, word for word from memory. The telling is intact; I insist on that, whatever happens to my fingers.
host.callback: I remember sharing the robber bridegroom's tale. A dreadful host, but a wonderfully alert visitor; she had more backbone than he bargained for.
host.callbackShort: That robber bridegroom made a grim argument for checking the guesthouse first.

title: Jikininki
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Buddhist karmic punishment and rites for the dead.
premise: A stranded priest spends the night beside a corpse and witnesses what comes to feed.

host.introduction: My old patron Lafcadio Hearn brought me Jikininki. I let him finish supper first; even an old ghoul like me knows when to clear the plates.
host.teaser: A priest arrives in a remote village after a death. Everyone leaves for the night, but he remains beside the body. Local customs can make wonderfully unsettling dinner conversation.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to keep this priest company through the night?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I'll serve the words exactly as I remember them, word for word. This memory is the one thing time hasn't taken a bite from.
host.callback: Jikininki was the tale I shared with you. That empty village had extraordinary arrangements for the night shift; I much prefer having your company here.
host.callbackShort: Jikininki gave that village a truly ghastly night shift.

title: Blue Beard
author: Charles Perrault; in Andrew Lang (editor)
advisories: Multiple murdered wives, blood and hanging corpses, threatened beheading, violent rescue.
premise: A new bride opens a forbidden room and learns what happened to the wives before her.

host.introduction: My old patron Andrew Lang brought this English telling of Charles Perrault's Blue Beard. One forbidden room! Nothing perks up my remains like suspicious hospitality.
host.teaser: A wealthy husband gives his new bride the keys to his house, with one room forbidden. The little key is terribly tempting. Some household rules have a nasty undertaker's signature about them.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we investigate that ominous little key?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: I'll recall this English telling word for word. My memory keeps its keys where I can find them, unlike my left kneecap.
host.callback: Blue Beard's locked room was the tale I shared. He had a mansion full of riches and not a single hospitable bone in his body.
host.callbackShort: Blue Beard's smallest key carried the gravest responsibility.

title: Morella
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A husband’s dread of his learned wife continues after her death through his growing daughter.
