host.callback: I shared the long gallery's twins with you. That tale found the tender place beneath my ribs; even old hauntings deserve a little kindness with their welcome.
host.callbackShort: The long gallery showed there can be warmth among the coldest shadows.

title: The Wind in the Rose-Bush
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: An aunt visiting her niece meets a succession of explanations that do not match what the house reveals.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman, an old patron, brought this family visit. She could make a rustling garden set my bones tapping against the bar.
host.teaser: An aunt comes to visit her niece and hears repeated explanations for the girl's absence. Small disturbances in the house and garden encourage more questions. Some family matters resist being quietly buried.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we listen to the uneasy whispers around this rose-bush?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll repeat Freeman word for word from memory. Every small sign remains; age has taken my cartilage, but never my attention to a guest's story.
host.callback: Freeman's rose-bush was the tale I shared with you. Such a quiet insistence on being heard; I keep an ear open, while I still have two.
host.callbackShort: That rose-bush gave quiet family questions a grave urgency.

title: Luella Miller
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: Neighbors puzzle over why caring for one charming, helpless woman seems to drain everyone around her.

host.introduction: My old patron Mary E. Wilkins Freeman brought me Luella Miller. A charming woman with exhausting demands; by the end, even my spare bones needed a lie-down.
host.teaser: Luella Miller always needs someone to care for her. Neighbors notice her helpers growing weaker, and one observer remembers the pattern. Being helpful can become a dreadfully draining occupation.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to meet this dangerously demanding neighbor?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll recall Freeman word for word. My memory still has plenty of life in it; fortunately, Luella never got her hands on that.
host.callback: Luella Miller's history was our tale. Such dreadful dependence; I prefer to leave my guests with good company and a story, instead of making them dead tired.
host.callbackShort: Luella Miller put a ghastly amount of weight on a little help.

title: Number 13
author: M. R. James
advisories: old religious conflict and suspected sorcery.
premise: A hotel guest investigates a room that seems to exist only after dark.

host.introduction: M. R. James, my old patron, brought a Danish hotel's curious arithmetic. An extra room after dark; lovely news for the night shift, alarming news for the occupants.
host.teaser: A hotel guest notices a room that seems absent by daylight. After dark, the corridor's numbers and neighbors become difficult to explain. A booking can develop some wonderfully grave complications.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we investigate this hotel's mysterious extra door?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I'll recall James word for word. Every number stays put in my memory; it's a better-built lodging than this creaking rib cage.
host.callback: Number 13 was the room I shared with you. Such inventive accommodation; I do appreciate a building that can squeeze in an extra haunting after sunset.
host.callbackShort: Number 13 gave the night clerk some gloriously ghastly arithmetic.

title: The Stalls of Barchester Cathedral
author: M. R. James
premise: A clergyman’s private papers connect unsettling carved figures with a hidden crime.

host.introduction: My old patron M. R. James brought an archdeacon's unsettling papers. Beautiful carvings, dreadful suspicions; enough to put a splendid creak in these old bones.
host.teaser: An obituary and diary trace an archdeacon's growing unease. Carved figures in his cathedral seem increasingly important. Old wood can carry more than decorative flourishes and a respectable coating of funeral dust.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to examine these ominous cathedral carvings?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I'll repeat James word for word from memory. The whole account is preserved; I leave the suspicious carving to the woodwork.
host.callback: I shared the Barchester carvings with you. Such beautifully dreadful furniture; I admire craftsmanship that can put a chill through the owner's bones.
host.callbackShort: Those Barchester carvings gave fine woodwork a truly grave reputation.

title: The Birthmark
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
premise: A scientist becomes convinced that he can remove the one tiny mark on his wife’s otherwise perfect face.

host.introduction: Nathaniel Hawthorne, an old patron, brought a scientist obsessed with perfection. Heh, one look at my face would have buried the poor fellow in paperwork.
host.teaser: A scientist believes he can erase a small birthmark from his wife's face. His confidence in the experiment grows. The pursuit of perfection has acquired a most unpleasant laboratory smell.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I share this troubling experiment in perfection?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll recall Hawthorne word for word. Every word remains as given; I know better than to perform cosmetic surgery on a good story.
host.callback: The Birthmark was the experiment I shared with you. I have a soft spot for imperfections; without mine, there'd be very little of this bartender left.
host.callbackShort: Hawthorne's birthmark tale makes me positively fond of my crooked remains.

title: The Mask
author: Robert W. Chambers
premise: An artist demonstrates a fluid that turns living things into flawless marble.

host.introduction: Robert W. Chambers, my old patron, brought an astonishing artist's discovery. Life turned to marble! My embalmer would have been green with professional envy.
host.teaser: An artist discovers a liquid that turns living things into flawless marble. His friends marvel, while affection complicates life around the studio. Beauty has acquired an unsettling capacity to stand perfectly still.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to visit this unnervingly inventive studio?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll remember Chambers word for word. The words are preserved without being petrified; I prefer a lively tale with my grave company.
host.callback: I shared Chambers's marble experiment with you. Such extraordinary preservation; enough to make an old ghoul feel positively underdressed in ordinary decomposing skin.
host.callbackShort: Chambers's marble experiment gave preservation a wonderfully chilling new finish.

title: The Old House in Vauxhall Walk
author: Charlotte Riddell
premise: A young man who has fallen on hard times takes shelter in an old house with an unresolved history.

host.introduction: Charlotte Riddell, an old patron, brought me a London shelter with a history. An empty house is never quite empty enough to bore these old bones.
host.teaser: A young man with nowhere to sleep enters an apparently empty house. Visions of former occupants and their money interrupt his rest. Free lodging sometimes comes with a very grave set of conditions.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear what stirs inside this old London house?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I'll recall Riddell word for word. Every room remains furnished in my memory; a few might have acquired the odd cobweb.
host.callback: That old house in Vauxhall Walk was our shelter in the tale. A remarkable night's lodging; enough buried history to keep an undertaker awake.
host.callbackShort: Vauxhall Walk offered a roof with a grave amount of history attached.

title: The Tractate Middoth
author: M. R. James
premise: A librarian’s search for an old book draws him into an inheritance dispute and a haunting.

host.introduction: M. R. James, my old patron, brought me a hazardous library errand. Dust, old books, and anxious readers; everything an aging ghoul needs for a lively evening.
host.teaser: A librarian searches for an old volume sought by competing readers. Something inside matters to a family's inheritance. The shelves have attracted an interest that feels rather too persistent for ordinary scholarship.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to open this library's unsettling little mystery?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I'll recall James word for word. My memory never loses a volume, though my spine needs rebinding.
host.callback: The Tractate Middoth was the book I shared with you. Such devoted readership; I admire an old volume that can keep its company well beyond closing time.
host.callbackShort: The Tractate Middoth had a reader with a decidedly grave attachment.

title: The Lost Ghost
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: Women sharing village news recall a forlorn child who appeared in a boarding house looking for her mother.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman, my old patron, brought a lost child's haunting. I kept the welcome warm; a small ghost deserves more than an old ghoul's clattering teeth.
host.teaser: Women recalling a boarding house describe a pale child who appeared looking for her mother. The household is frightened, but the little visitor seems terribly lost. Some hauntings need warmth more than a locked door.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I share this sorrowful little visitor's story?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: I'll remember Freeman word for word. Every word is handled gently; these old bony hands can still take care of something precious.
host.callback: I shared Freeman's lost little ghost with you. That welcome reaches the warm corner beneath my ribs; there is room at this bar for tender hauntings too.
host.callbackShort: Freeman's lost ghost reached the soft spot in this old skeleton.

title: An Engineer’s Story
author: Amelia B. Edwards
premise: An engineer’s account of friendship and betrayal reaches a crisis on a railway journey.

host.introduction: Amelia B. Edwards brought this railway tale to my bar. Heh! Friendship, jealousy, and a journey that nearly derailed my jaw.
host.teaser: Two childhood friends become railway men, until jealousy threatens their bond. One dangerous night puts private fury beside a train full of lives. An excellent time to keep every skeleton off the tracks.
host.offerQuestion: Fancy a railway tale with some grave complications?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Edwards’s tale, word for word, coming right up. My memory never goes off the rails; several of my ribs already have.
host.callback: That engineer’s account we shared puts a dreadful strain on friendship. I still admire the way Edwards brings a buried grievance roaring down the line.
host.callbackShort: The engineer’s friendship had some dangerously sharp points. Heh!

title: The Treasure of Abbot Thomas
author: M. R. James
advisories: Integral Latin and cipher passages make this more demanding to read or narrate.
premise: A scholar follows a cryptic inscription toward hidden treasure and its guardian.

host.introduction: My old patron M. R. James brought me a treasure hunt. Gold, old stone, grave withdrawal penalties—what a delightful little investment!
host.teaser: A scholar follows clues in stained glass and old writing toward hidden gold. The man who buried it was thorough about security. Some fortunes deserve to remain dead money.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we follow those clues toward the buried fortune?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: I’ll tell James’s story word for word. My memory is a splendid vault; even the worms haven’t found the combination.
host.callback: Abbot Thomas’s treasure hunt was a lovely grave investment. I still prefer tips that arrive without a subterranean guardian.
host.callbackShort: Abbot Thomas’s gold came with a truly grave security deposit.

title: The Plattner Story
author: H. G. Wells
premise: A chemistry accident leaves a schoolteacher strangely altered and carrying memories of another world.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells once brought this strange experiment to my bar. A body turned round the wrong way! I checked my own joints before pouring.
host.teaser: A schoolteacher vanishes during a chemistry experiment and returns strangely reversed. His account describes another world beside our own. Heh, even the afterlife may have a wrong entrance.
host.offerQuestion: Care to follow Plattner into that peculiar other world?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Wells’s words, word for word. My memory remains the right way round, whatever the rest of this elderly carcass gets up to.
host.callback: Plattner’s journey gave us a most unusual view of the hereafter. I keep my bones in their usual order; inventory is troublesome enough already.
host.callbackShort: Plattner certainly put a new twist on coming back. Ha!

title: The Southwest Chamber
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: Boarders cycle through a room in which a recently deceased relative’s presence seems impossible to dismiss.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman told me this across the bar. A troublesome bedroom! I know coffins with a more welcoming atmosphere.
host.teaser: Two sisters take in boarders, but one bedroom seems determined to change its occupants’ habits. A forceful former resident may still have opinions. Death apparently failed to terminate the lease.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like a look inside that stubbornly haunted room?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Freeman’s words, exactly as I heard them. My memory never evicts a good tale; there’s always room among the cobwebs.
host.callback: The southwest chamber we visited certainly took possession seriously. I enjoy a spirited guest, but choosing everyone else’s habits is dreadful hospitality.
host.callbackShort: That southwest chamber had a landlord beyond the grave. Heh!

title: Rappaccini's Daughter
author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
premise: A student becomes fascinated by a young woman who lives among her father’s extraordinary poisonous plants.

host.introduction: My old patron Nathaniel Hawthorne brought me this poisonous garden. Such exquisite flowers! I admired them from behind my remaining nose.
host.teaser: A student admires a young woman tending her father’s extraordinary poisonous plants. As he draws closer, fascination and suspicion grow together. Romance has found a particularly unhealthy place to put down roots.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I introduce you to Rappaccini’s unsettling garden?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Hawthorne’s tale, word for word. My memory preserves every petal; embalming would only spoil the fragrance.
host.callback: Rappaccini’s garden gave us a remarkable bouquet of love and suspicion. I keep that tale well preserved; some flowers belong in a story, however gorgeous the funeral arrangement.
host.callbackShort: Rappaccini’s flowers made romance a decidedly grave undertaking.

title: The Open Door
author: Charlotte Riddell
premise: A young clerk tries to earn a reward by solving the mystery of a door that will not stay shut.

host.introduction: Charlotte Riddell was an old patron with a marvelous tale of easy money. A door that won’t close! Even my coffin grants me more privacy.
host.teaser: A young clerk hopes to earn a reward by solving a country house’s stubbornly open door. He agrees to keep watch. There may be more than a draught refusing to rest in peace.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we investigate that door and its unfinished business?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Riddell’s words, word for word, with nothing shut out. My memory has hinges far better preserved than these knees.
host.callback: That door at Ladlow Hall gave us some splendid unfinished business. Heh! I admire a house that refuses to bury the matter quietly.
host.callbackShort: Ladlow Hall’s door simply wouldn’t let the past rest.

title: The Juniper-Tree
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm; translated by Margaret Hunt
advisories: Child beheading, family cannibalism, abusive parent, fatal crushing.
premise: A murdered boy returns in bird form, singing his story and arranging vengeance.

host.introduction: My old patrons Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm brought this collected tale in Margaret Hunt’s English. A juniper tree and a song with grave family connections!
host.teaser: Cruelty enters a family home, and a beautiful bird begins singing an unsettling song nearby. Some family secrets refuse to stay buried—especially the ones with such excellent lungs.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear what stirs beneath the juniper tree?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Margaret Hunt’s English telling, word for word. Every note survives in my memory; the worms have never managed to eat a chorus.
host.callback: The juniper tree’s song gave us quite a family reckoning. I appreciate a memorable performance, though that bird arranged a particularly crushing encore.
host.callbackShort: That juniper bird knew how to bring a family secret up.

title: In the Court of the Dragon
author: Robert W. Chambers
premise: A churchgoer senses that an organist’s attention is following him far beyond the service.

host.introduction: Robert W. Chambers shared this tale at my bar. An organist with a dreadful sense of pursuit! I do love a funeral march that goes places.
host.teaser: A churchgoer notices a disturbing organist and soon feels pursued through ordinary streets. Behind the encounter lurks a dangerous book. This melody has an unpleasant way of following the audience home.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I play out that sinister pursuit for you?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Chambers’s words, word for word. My memory keeps perfect time, even though my heart abandoned the rhythm long ago.
host.callback: The Court of the Dragon gave us an organist who took his audience seriously. Heh! An encore is generally nicer when it waits to be invited.
host.callbackShort: That organist’s pursuit had a wonderfully dreadful rhythm.

title: The Story of Mimi-Nashi-Hōichi
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: War dead and drowned children, ears torn off, Buddhist protective writing/ritual.
premise: A blind musician performs for an unseen court that has a terrible connection to a nearby cemetery.

host.introduction: Lafcadio Hearn, an old guest of mine, brought this account of Hōichi’s music. Such devoted listeners! Some audiences refuse to let death interrupt the entertainment.
host.teaser: A gifted blind musician receives nighttime invitations to perform for a distinguished gathering. His listeners want him back, but a friend grows worried. It may be time to examine the guest list.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear about Hōichi’s mysterious audience?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Hearn’s telling, word for word. My memory holds every note; a skull can have lovely acoustics when properly occupied.
host.callback: Hōichi’s midnight audience certainly gave us a haunting performance. I adore appreciative company, but even the dead ought to know when to let a musician go home.
host.callbackShort: Hōichi’s listeners took their appreciation well beyond the grave.

title: Caterpillars
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A guest at an Italian villa sees horrible creatures in a supposedly empty bedroom.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson described this Italian villa over my bar. Then came the caterpillars. Ha, I nearly crawled out of what remains of my skin!
host.teaser: A visitor sees grotesque caterpillars swarming in an apparently empty bedroom. An interest in insects takes an increasingly dreadful turn. This is a creeping tale of illness as well as unwanted company.
host.offerQuestion: Care to investigate the villa’s particularly unpleasant visitors?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Benson’s account, word for word. Nothing has crawled out of my memory, though I occasionally hear scratching near the back.
host.callback: Those villa caterpillars made a wonderfully dreadful addition to our collection. Even I prefer my creeping visitors safely between the pages.
host.callbackShort: Benson’s villa had an especially unhealthy case of the creeps.

title: Rokuro-Kubi
author: Lafcadio Hearn
advisories: Detached heads, threats of cannibalism, fighting, corpse/head display, Buddhist rites.
premise: A traveling priest accepts shelter and discovers that his hosts’ heads roam without their bodies.

host.introduction: Lafcadio Hearn brought this mountain lodging tale to my bar. Such unconventional hosts! I checked that my own head was still attached before thanking him.
host.teaser: A traveling priest accepts shelter in a remote cottage. When he wakes, something seems badly amiss with the sleeping household. Heh, hospitality can have a rather loose attachment to the usual arrangements.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we spend a little time with those unusual hosts?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I’d love to hear it.
host.bridge: Hearn’s words, word for word. I keep this tale in my head, and my head firmly on the premises.
host.callback: The roaming heads of Rokuro-Kubi gave us a splendidly disorderly household. I love welcoming guests, but I prefer to greet all their parts at once.
host.callbackShort: That mountain household really knew how to get ahead. Ha!

title: The Music of Erich Zann
author: H. P. Lovecraft
advisories: Historical terminology for a person who does not speak.
premise: A lodger investigates the strange music an old violinist plays in his attic at night.

host.introduction: H. P. Lovecraft once told me about Erich Zann across this bar. Strange attic music! It made my teeth chatter in entirely unfamiliar keys.
host.teaser: A lodger grows fascinated by an old musician’s extraordinary nighttime playing. Inside the attic, the musician seems deeply anxious about his window. Some performances are best heard with the curtains firmly drawn.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear Erich Zann’s unsettling tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Lovecraft’s words, exactly as I heard them. My memory has never missed a note; my teeth handle any unwanted percussion.
host.callback: Erich Zann’s attic gave us quite a performance. I still admire that music’s terrible urgency; it could rattle a whole cemetery without waking the neighbors politely.
host.callbackShort: Erich Zann’s music had the bones for a dreadful concert.

title: The Toll-House
author: W. W. Jacobs
premise: Four friends spend the night in a house said to exact a deadly toll.

host.introduction: My old patron W. W. Jacobs brought this tale of four confident friends. A haunted house for the night! Such an economical way to book a fright.
host.teaser: Four friends spend a night in a house said to demand a deadly toll. Laughter gives way to darkness and uncertainty. The difficulty is knowing when the joke has stopped being a joke.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear what that toll-house charges its visitors?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Jacobs’s tale, word for word. My memory collects every detail; fortunately, it accepts payment in attention rather than bones.
host.callback: Our night at the toll-house gave us a ghastly reckoning. Heh! I prefer an evening whose charges fit on a cocktail menu.
host.callbackShort: The toll-house made a dreadful business of its overnight guests.

title: The Moonlit Road
author: Ambrose Bierce
premise: Three accounts of a family tragedy reveal that the living and the dead may understand it very differently.

host.introduction: Ambrose Bierce brought three accounts of one tragedy to my bar. I listened to every voice; the grave should never hog the conversation.
host.teaser: A son, a troubled wanderer, and a voice beyond death describe the same family tragedy. Their stories do not quite agree. Even the dead can have a dreadful failure to communicate.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear all three voices along the moonlit road?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Bierce’s words, word for word, with each voice intact. My memory keeps excellent company on both sides of the grave.
host.callback: The moonlit road gave us three voices and a terrible misunderstanding. I’m always glad to hear a guest out; burying a conversation early can cause such trouble.
host.callbackShort: Those three moonlit accounts had some grave differences of opinion.

title: The Sea Raiders
author: H. G. Wells
premise: Holidaymakers on the English coast face an invasion of unfamiliar carnivorous sea creatures.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells brought this seaside outing to my bar. Heh! Nothing spoils a holiday quite like discovering you’re on somebody else’s menu.
host.teaser: A man strolling along the English coast notices unfamiliar creatures among the rocks. His pleasant outing becomes an urgent warning to other holidaymakers. The seaside has developed a distinctly unhealthy appetite.
host.offerQuestion: Care to hear what disturbed that coastal afternoon?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Wells’s tale, word for word. My memory keeps every morsel intact; I leave the chewing to the creatures.
host.callback: Those sea raiders gave us a dreadful seaside excursion. I’m delighted to have company here, where a guest belongs at the table rather than on the menu.
host.callbackShort: The sea raiders put a ghastly twist on seaside dining.

title: Gavon’s Eve
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A fishing holiday leads visitors toward a local pool and a night when the dead may answer.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson once told me this beside the bar. A fishing holiday and a pool with grave connections! I put away the net and listened.
host.teaser: A troubled young man is drawn to a pool and an old nighttime observance. His friends investigate what happens there after dark. Some invitations sound terribly tempting when they promise company from the grave.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we listen beside the pool on Gavon’s Eve?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Benson’s words, word for word. I’ve kept this night floating in my memory; even the grave couldn’t sink it.
host.callback: Gavon’s pool gave us a dreadful midnight appointment. I enjoy a little company from beyond, but I prefer visitors who come through the front door.
host.callbackShort: Gavon’s Eve made fishing for company a grave undertaking.

title: The Other Bed
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A guest in a Swiss hotel becomes increasingly conscious of the unused bed in his room.

host.introduction: My old patron E. F. Benson described a Swiss hotel with a spare bed. I adore extra accommodation, provided the occupant has actually departed.
host.teaser: A winter hotel guest becomes uneasy about the unused bed beside his own. The staff seem reluctant to enter. Rest assured, this tale has very little interest in restful accommodation.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to investigate that unsettling spare bed?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Benson’s tale, word for word. My memory never sleeps; I leave all that lying still to the rest of me.
host.callback: That other bed gave us a dreadful rooming arrangement. Heh! A coffin for one is beginning to look positively sociable by comparison.
host.callbackShort: The Swiss hotel’s spare bed had a grave occupancy problem.

title: The Well
author: W. W. Jacobs
premise: A man trying to hide a crime finds himself drawn back to the place where he concealed it.

host.introduction: W. W. Jacobs told me this grim little account across the bar. A secret down a well! People do choose the most inconvenient places to bury trouble.
host.teaser: A man conceals a terrible secret in a well. Then a request to retrieve a bracelet threatens to bring it to light. Guilt has chosen a dreadfully damp hiding place.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we look into that well and its buried secret?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Jacobs’s words, word for word. My memory keeps everything above water, which is more than some of his characters can manage.
host.callback: The well gave us a particularly deep problem of concealment. I keep thinking what a nuisance ordinary lost property becomes when there’s already a skeleton in storage.
host.callbackShort: That well’s secret gave ordinary curiosity a dreadful depth.

title: Canon Alberic’s Scrap-book
author: M. R. James
premise: An antiquarian buys a remarkable old scrapbook and discovers why its owner wanted to part with it.

host.introduction: M. R. James once brought me a tale of a bargain scrapbook. Such fine old paper! I know a thing or two about alarming preservation.
host.teaser: An antiquarian finds a remarkable scrapbook and a seller strangely eager to part with it. One drawing deserves particular attention. Some bargains come with a little more presence than the buyer requested.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we open Canon Alberic’s unusual scrapbook?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: James’s words, word for word. My memory keeps every leaf intact; paper and old bartenders deserve careful preservation.
host.callback: Canon Alberic’s scrapbook was a splendidly dreadful bargain. I remember sharing it with you; the seller’s eagerness still deserves a place in the appraisal.
host.callbackShort: Canon Alberic’s scrapbook had a fiendish idea of added value.

title: The Mezzotint
author: M. R. James
premise: A dull country-house print begins to show details that were not there before.

host.introduction: My old patron M. R. James described a dull print of a house. Then the details changed—ha, art with a pulse problem!
host.teaser: A collector receives an ordinary print of a country house. Viewers begin noticing details that were not there earlier. The picture seems to have a story to tell, and it refuses to hold its pose.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to watch that peculiar picture unfold?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: James’s tale, word for word. My memory never alters the picture, however much the picture resents staying still.
host.callback: That changing mezzotint made a marvelous grave impression. I’m fond of lively décor, but a picture ought to ask before rearranging its own company.
host.callbackShort: The mezzotint gave us a frightful moving picture. Heh!

title: Count Magnus
author: M. R. James
advisories: A tentative historical remark about national reserve.
premise: A traveler’s interest in a sinister nobleman’s tomb becomes dangerously personal.

host.introduction: M. R. James brought Count Magnus to my bar in a tale. I adore an old nobleman with grave connections, provided he arrives on the page.
host.teaser: A traveler researching a Swedish family grows fascinated by a sinister nobleman’s sealed tomb. He returns, asks questions, and wishes for more knowledge. Curiosity may be knocking rather too enthusiastically.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear about that traveler’s interest in Count Magnus?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: James’s words, word for word. My memory keeps its tombs well catalogued; a misplaced count can spoil an entire evening.
host.callback: Count Magnus gave us a splendidly dreadful lesson in curiosity. Heh! I enjoy an interested guest, though a sealed tomb is a questionable place to seek one.
host.callbackShort: Count Magnus took an awfully grave interest in his admirer.

title: From the Dead
author: E. Nesbit
advisories: Idealized romance and period relationship assumptions.
premise: A bitter misunderstanding between lovers has consequences that seem to outlast death.

host.introduction: E. Nesbit shared this tale with me across the bar. One letter, such dreadful damage! Even an old ghoul knows when a heart needs careful handling.
host.teaser: A man reads a letter suggesting his fiancée loves someone else. His response opens a terrible breach between them. Some unfinished business refuses to lie quietly in the grave.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear this troubled return from the dead?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Nesbit’s tale, word for word. My memory keeps these fragile things intact; being dead needn’t mean being careless.
host.callback: From the Dead gave us a terribly sorrowful reunion. I keep a welcome ready for returning company; a door needn’t wait for a funeral before it opens.
host.callbackShort: That reunion in From the Dead left love with grave unfinished business.

title: The Room in the Tower
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A recurring nightmare about a sinister guest room begins to resemble waking life.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson described this nightmare at my bar. The same dreadful room, again and again! I usually call that a permanent reservation.
host.teaser: A man repeatedly dreams of a house party and a sinister room in a tower. Then a real visit starts to resemble the dream. Something seems determined to honor his reservation.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear about that dreadful room in the tower?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Benson’s words, word for word. My memory has kept the room exactly as it was; the cobwebs are merely complimentary.
host.callback: The room in the tower gave us a ghastly welcome. I love recognizing a returning guest, but that invitation took familiarity several graves too far.
host.callbackShort: That tower room kept its nightmare reservation with dreadful efficiency.

title: The Shadows on the Wall
author: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman
premise: After a household death, a shadow on the sitting-room wall refuses to obey ordinary rules.

host.introduction: Mary E. Wilkins Freeman told me this while I tended the bar. A shadow that won’t behave! Mine at least has the decency to look half dead.
host.teaser: After a family death, three sisters notice a shadow that refuses to behave like an ordinary shadow. Their brother offers explanations. The wall seems unwilling to let the matter rest in peace.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear what those shadows suggest?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Freeman’s words, word for word. My memory casts no substitutes; I’ve kept every dreadful detail in the proper light.
host.callback: Those shadows on the wall gave us a family history that wouldn’t stay buried. Ha! Some rooms insist on displaying their skeletons without bothering with a cupboard.
host.callbackShort: Freeman’s wall gave the family secret a truly grave outline.

title: Man-Size in Marble
author: E. Nesbit
premise: A couple living near an old church hear a local warning about two stone figures on All Saints’ Eve.

host.introduction: E. Nesbit brought this Halloween tale to my bar. Marble figures and a nervous housekeeper! I do love decorations that take the season seriously.
host.teaser: A country couple hears a warning about two marble figures in the local church. Their housekeeper refuses to stay on All Saints’ Eve. Apparently, some stone gentlemen have troubling Halloween plans.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we spend Halloween with those unsettling marble figures?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Nesbit’s tale, word for word. My memory is set in stone; fortunately, it has better manners than certain statues.
host.callback: Those marble figures gave us a dreadful Halloween appointment. I’m fond of seasonal visitors, but I’d have offered that sensible housekeeper a very comfortable seat here.
host.callbackShort: Nesbit’s marble figures took Halloween into their own stony hands.

title: The Ash-tree
author: M. R. James
premise: Deaths at an old country house draw attention to a tree beside a bedroom window.

host.introduction: My old patron M. R. James brought me this country estate. A house, a tree, an accusation! What fertile soil for a grave misunderstanding.
host.teaser: Strange deaths at a country house draw attention to an ash-tree beside a bedroom window. An old accusation casts a long shadow. The garden may have something dreadful taking root.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to investigate what troubles that ash-tree?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: James’s words, word for word. My memory preserves every root of the matter; the rest of me makes excellent mulch.
host.callback: The ash-tree gave us an exceptionally nasty family of branches. I remain delighted by James’s talent for making landscaping a grave concern.
host.callbackShort: That ash-tree had a dreadful way of branching into the bedroom.

title: The Premature Burial
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A narrator consumed by fear of being buried alive recounts cases that make the fear feel plausible.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe once described this fear at my bar. Premature burial! I prefer to arrive fashionably late to my own funeral.
host.teaser: A man terrified of being buried alive collects alarming cases and plans elaborate safeguards. Every precaution feeds his fear. Heh, this is someone taking his final accommodation very personally.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we examine Poe’s precautions against an early burial?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Poe’s words, word for word. My memory hasn’t buried a single detail, despite several enthusiastic attempts by the worms.
host.callback: The Premature Burial gave us some very grave advance planning. I admire a careful guest, though I’d recommend choosing a bar seat before ordering a coffin.
host.callbackShort: Poe’s burial precautions took being early to a dreadful extreme.

title: The Cat
author: E. F. Benson
advisories: bloody throat injury and possible self-harm.
premise: A painter notices troubling connections among an old love, a portrait, and a cat.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson brought this painter’s troubles to my bar. An old romance, a portrait, a cat! Such a charming collection of grave complications.
host.teaser: A successful painter’s life grows unsettled by an old romance, a portrait, and a cat. His confidence begins to fray. This dark tale includes animal harm; its claws reach well beyond the canvas.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear the painter’s disturbing tale?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Benson’s account, word for word. My memory keeps every brushstroke, though the cat would probably prefer to scratch the frame.
host.callback: That painter’s portrait and the cat gave us a grisly composition. I favor a quieter still life, preferably one that stays still after closing.
host.callbackShort: The painter’s cat put some dreadful claws into the picture.

title: The Yellow Wallpaper
author: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
premise: Confined to a room for a prescribed rest cure, a woman becomes absorbed by the pattern on its walls.

host.introduction: Charlotte Perkins Gilman told me this across the bar. I gave her every moment she needed; being a ghoul is no excuse for burying somebody’s voice.
host.teaser: A woman prescribed a rest cure keeps a secret account of her confinement. The wallpaper increasingly absorbs her attention. Even my coffin offers more say in the decorating.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear the woman’s private account?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Gilman’s words, word for word, with room for her voice. My memory has better preservation standards than those dreadful walls.
host.callback: The Yellow Wallpaper gave us a room that was anything but restful. I still keep an attentive ear for its narrator; listening is one duty death hasn’t excused me from.
host.callbackShort: That wallpaper’s pattern made a truly dreadful prison lining.

title: The Empty House
author: Algernon Blackwood
premise: A man and his adventurous aunt spend a night exploring a house associated with a murder.

host.introduction: Algernon Blackwood brought me this after-hours house inspection. An adventurous aunt with keys! I adore a guest who arrives ready to disturb the dust.
host.teaser: A man and his adventurous aunt explore an empty house with a murderous history. As they move through the rooms, the place grows less reassuring. Somebody may have forgotten to tell the house it’s vacant.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we join that aunt’s unsettling house inspection?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Blackwood’s tale, word for word. My memory keeps every room in order; the skeletons occasionally complain about the dusting.
host.callback: Shorthouse and his aunt gave us a magnificent empty-house inspection. Heh! Some properties come fully furnished with matters that refuse to rest.
host.callbackShort: Shorthouse’s aunt certainly found a house with grave character.

title: The Stolen Body
author: H. G. Wells
advisories: Historical mental-health vocabulary; violent assaults on adults and a child.
premise: An experiment in leaving the body gives an intruder an opportunity to move in.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells once told me about a gentleman leaving his body unattended. I tightened my vest immediately; this carcass may be shabby, but it’s occupied.
host.teaser: An experiment lets a man leave his body, but something else notices the vacancy. Soon London notices the consequences. Heh, a brief absence can become a dreadful dispute over the furniture.
host.offerQuestion: Shall I tell you about that stolen body?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Wells’s words, word for word. My memory remains in residence, and I refuse to sublet even the dustiest corner.
host.callback: The Stolen Body gave us a frightful case of unauthorized occupancy. I’m always glad to welcome company, but guests really should bring their own skeletons.
host.callbackShort: That stolen body had a dreadful tenant problem. Ha!

title: Smith: An Episode in a Lodging-House
author: Algernon Blackwood
premise: A medical student becomes suspicious of the secretive activities of a fellow lodger.

host.introduction: Algernon Blackwood was an old patron with a marvelous lodging-house story. A secretive neighbor and late experiments! No wonder the rent gets paid in dread.
host.teaser: A medical student becomes curious about a fellow lodger’s books and private experiments. A scholarly favor draws him closer. Some neighbors take opening doors to possibilities rather too literally.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear about the lodger called Smith?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Blackwood’s words, word for word. My memory keeps the account securely housed; nothing gets summoned into a sentence without permission.
host.callback: Smith gave us a deeply inconvenient neighbor. I enjoy lively company, but an occult experiment after closing really ought to come with a courtesy note.
host.callbackShort: Smith’s lodging-house had a dreadful case of neighborly spirits.

title: The Story of the Late Mr. Elvesham
author: H. G. Wells
premise: A poor student receives an offer from a rich older man whose generosity has disturbing conditions.

host.introduction: H. G. Wells brought Mr. Elvesham’s generous offer to my bar. I leaned forward. An inheritance with grave conditions always deserves a good, bony look.
host.teaser: A struggling student receives an extraordinary inheritance offer from a wealthy stranger. A luxurious dinner follows. Heh, this gift may require rather more of the recipient than a thank-you note.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear what Mr. Elvesham’s generosity involves?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Wells’s words, word for word. My memory preserves all the conditions; a good ghoul reads the fine print before the epitaph.
host.callback: Mr. Elvesham’s offer gave us a fiendish lesson in generosity. I remain fond of gifts that leave the recipient in possession of the usual essentials.
host.callbackShort: Mr. Elvesham made that inheritance a terribly personal affair.

title: The Fall of the House of Usher
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A visitor arrives at a decaying mansion where his old friend and the house seem bound to the same sickness.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe brought the House of Usher to my bar in a tale. Splendid decay! At last, a building with a complexion to match mine.
host.teaser: A visitor answers an old friend’s invitation to a decaying mansion. Illness, music, and family history fill its rooms. The building itself seems burdened by the same dreadful inheritance as its occupants.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to enter the House of Usher with me?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Poe’s tale, word for word. My memory preserves the whole house; the foundations are another matter entirely.
host.callback: Our tale of the House of Usher had a magnificent air of decay. I still admire Poe’s ability to give a building such grave family responsibilities.
host.callbackShort: Usher’s house carried its family troubles right into the foundations.

title: An Episode of Cathedral History
author: M. R. James
premise: Repairs to a cathedral disturb a tomb and the thing associated with it.

host.introduction: My old patron M. R. James described these cathedral repairs. Disturbing an ancient tomb! Some renovations really do bring the neighborhood back to life.
host.teaser: Repairs expose an old cathedral tomb, and a boy notices something through a narrow opening. Later accounts piece together the trouble. The workmen may have underestimated the existing occupant’s interest in the plans.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we uncover that unsettling episode of cathedral history?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: James’s account, word for word. My memory preserves old buildings beautifully; it knows better than to knock through the occupied walls.
host.callback: Those cathedral repairs gave us a dreadful lesson in preservation. I appreciate improvements, but an ancient tomb deserves a knock before anyone moves the furniture.
host.callbackShort: The cathedral’s renovation had some grave structural consequences.

title: The Yellow Sign
author: Robert W. Chambers
premise: A painter and his model become disturbed by a cemetery watchman, recurring dreams and an unfamiliar symbol.

host.introduction: Robert W. Chambers brought this painter’s tale to my bar. A cemetery watchman and a mysterious keepsake! Some souvenirs come with remarkably grave baggage.
host.teaser: A painter and his model share disturbing dreams about a cemetery watchman. An unfamiliar symbol and a forbidden book deepen the unease. Something dreadful seems eager to make their acquaintance.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear about the mysterious Yellow Sign?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Chambers’s words, word for word. My memory keeps every sign in order; I’ve had enough trouble misplacing my own head.
host.callback: The Yellow Sign gave us some marvelously unwelcome company. I love a thoughtful keepsake, but a cemetery connection rather complicates the gift wrapping.
host.callbackShort: That Yellow Sign was a souvenir with grave attachments.

title: The Judge’s House
author: Bram Stoker
premise: A student rents an isolated house where a sinister portrait, rats, and a bell rope resist quiet study.

host.introduction: Bram Stoker once described this student’s quiet lodgings to me. A judge’s house, rats, a sinister portrait! I nearly cackled my jaw off before he finished.
host.teaser: A student rents an isolated judge’s house to study. The rats are bold, the portrait unsettling, and the bell rope has a history. Even the furnishings seem determined to interrupt his examination.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we spend a little time in the Judge’s House?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Stoker’s words, word for word. My memory never drops a line, even when the rope has such an alarming history.
host.callback: The Judge’s House gave us a dreadful place to study. I much prefer company at the bar; these stools offer a considerably friendlier seat of judgment.
host.callbackShort: That judge’s house took quiet study to a grave extreme.

title: Oh, Whistle, and I’ll Come to You, My Lad
author: M. R. James
premise: A professor finds a small old whistle on a coastal walk and sounds it.

host.introduction: M. R. James told me this while visiting my bar. A professor finds an old whistle! I do enjoy a souvenir with the power to raise company.
host.teaser: A professor finds an inscribed whistle near old coastal ruins and tries it. His holiday soon grows unsettled by a figure and disturbances in his room. Some invitations need only a little breath.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear what follows that professor’s whistle?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: James’s tale, word for word. My memory has all the original breath in it; my lungs are mostly for decorative purposes now.
host.callback: The professor’s whistle gave us a splendidly unwelcome visitor. Heh! I appreciate a summons, but I prefer one that comes with a reservation and a name.
host.callbackShort: That coastal whistle had a grave talent for attracting company.

title: With Intent to Steal
author: Algernon Blackwood
premise: A night in a barn proves less peaceful than the guest expects.

host.introduction: Algernon Blackwood brought me this tale of a night in a barn. Such rustic charm! The accommodations apparently included a dreadful interest in the guests.
host.teaser: Two men investigate a barn associated with a terrible death. One wants to explore fear and the human will. An overnight experiment is taking shape in a place with grave objections to peaceful sleep.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear about that unsettling night in the barn?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Blackwood’s words, word for word. My memory keeps the entire night intact; no sinister tenant gets to steal a sentence.
host.callback: That barn gave us a ghastly experiment in overnight hospitality. I’m delighted to offer company without asking anyone to bed down among the unfinished business.
host.callbackShort: Blackwood’s barn had dreadful ideas about possessing its visitors.

title: The Old Nurse’s Story
author: Elizabeth Gaskell
advisories: Child abuse and death by exposure.
premise: A nurse protecting a little girl in an old manor hears music and sees a child outside in the cold.

host.introduction: Elizabeth Gaskell told me this nurse’s tale at my bar. A snowy house with old secrets! I warmed to its fierce protector, though warming is mostly ceremonial for me.
host.teaser: A nurse and her young charge arrive at an old family house. An organ sounds without an apparent player, and a child appears outside in the snow. The past is pressing for admission.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear the old nurse’s winter haunting?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Gaskell’s tale, word for word. My memory keeps the nurse’s voice clear; the grave doesn’t get to have the last word on good care.
host.callback: The old nurse’s story gave us a brave protector amid the cold. I still have a soft spot for her care of Rosamond; unusual, given the state of my internal furnishings.
host.callbackShort: That old nurse had more backbone than the haunted household.

title: The Horla
author: Guy de Maupassant
premise: A man’s diary traces his growing belief that an unseen being has entered his house and begun controlling him.

host.introduction: Guy de Maupassant brought this invisible guest to my bar in a tale. Heh! I like to welcome everyone, but an empty chair should at least introduce itself.
host.teaser: A man records disturbed sleep, disappearing drinks, and a growing sense of an unseen presence. He begins testing what is happening. This houseguest may have a dreadful interest in more than the refreshments.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we follow the diarist’s search for the unseen Horla?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: This English telling, word for word. My memory keeps every entry visible; the author is Guy de Maupassant, whatever else may be lurking nearby.
host.callback: The Horla gave us a troubling case of unseen company. I enjoy a full bar, but I still prefer guests who announce themselves before investigating the refreshments.
host.callbackShort: The Horla made invisible company a grave domestic complication.

title: The Residence at Whitminster
author: M. R. James
premise: Old accounts of two boys at a cathedral residence reveal why certain objects were put away.

host.introduction: M. R. James brought the Whitminster papers to my bar. Two boys, old correspondence, locked doors! A beautifully preserved collection of reasons to mind the key.
host.teaser: Accounts from different years reveal disturbing events around two boys, a cathedral residence, and carefully stored objects. Some rooms have been left closed. The household appears to favor preserving its secrets under lock.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear what the Whitminster papers reveal?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: James’s words, word for word. My memory files everything carefully; even the skeletons have their proper drawers.
host.callback: Whitminster gave us some dreadful reasons for keeping objects locked away. I admire good preservation, especially when opening the collection might also invite it to mingle.
host.callbackShort: Whitminster’s locked collection had some very grave contents.

title: Mr Humphreys and his Inheritance
author: M. R. James
premise: An inherited country estate includes a maze whose center conceals a troubling history.

host.introduction: M. R. James told me about this inheritance over my bar. An estate with its own maze! How thoughtful to include so many possible dead ends.
host.teaser: An inherited estate includes a carefully designed maze and an odd object at its center. Its new owner consults old writing and draws a map. The dead ends may be the least of his difficulties.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we explore Mr. Humphreys’s mysterious inheritance?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: James’s tale, word for word. My memory never loses its way; even the cobwebs have been issued a map.
host.callback: Mr. Humphreys’s maze gave us an intricate grave concern. I prefer an inheritance whose paths stay politely where the gardener put them.
host.callbackShort: That inherited maze gave dead ends a most unsettling meaning.

title: The Screaming Skull
author: F. Marion Crawford
premise: A retired seaman explains why the skull in his cupboard cannot simply be thrown away.

host.introduction: F. Marion Crawford told me this skull’s story at my bar. At last, an ornament with a voice! I nearly applauded with both remaining hands.
host.teaser: A retired captain inherits a cottage with an unwelcome skull. He insists he is practical, despite hearing screams. An old dinner conversation may have left something dreadful lodged among the household effects.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear the captain’s account of that skull?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Crawford’s words, word for word. My memory keeps a quieter skull than his captain’s, though the acoustics remain excellent.
host.callback: That screaming skull gave us a wonderfully vocal household problem. I enjoy a lively conversation, but an ornament really should wait until the guest has finished speaking.
host.callbackShort: The captain’s skull had a bone to pick with quiet evenings.

title: The Familiar
author: J. Sheridan Le Fanu
premise: A retired captain is pursued by an uncanny figure that seems to know his past.

host.introduction: J. Sheridan Le Fanu told me this captain’s tale across the bar. Persistent footsteps! I like returning company, but some guests make a grave art of following.
host.teaser: A retired captain notices a strange figure following him. The presence seems to know his past, and ordinary precautions offer little help. Old business may be coming back with a particularly determined tread.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we follow Captain Barton’s unsettling encounter?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Le Fanu’s words, word for word. My memory keeps every footstep; the rest of this old body is less reliably attached.
host.callback: Captain Barton’s familiar gave us a dreadful demonstration of persistence. I’m pleased when guests return; I simply prefer they let the host know when they plan to leave.
host.callbackShort: Captain Barton’s visitor had a grave talent for staying close.

title: Berenice
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A man’s obsessive attention settles on one small feature of his ailing cousin.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe brought Berenice’s tale to my bar. Such dreadful precision! I found myself taking a protective interest in my remaining teeth.
host.teaser: An obsessive man fixates on a small feature of his ailing cousin. As her illness worsens, his thoughts tighten their grip. This is dark bodily horror, with far more bite than a comfortable family visit.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear Poe’s deeply unsettling Berenice?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Poe’s words, word for word. My memory has lost fewer details than my jaw has teeth; every dreadful one remains accounted for.
host.callback: Berenice gave us an exceptionally grisly obsession. I still handle that tale with care; even a delighted old ghoul can recognize when something deserves a gentle introduction.
host.callbackShort: Poe’s Berenice put a dreadful bite into that family visit.

title: The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A mesmerist attempts to hold a dying man between life and death and records the result.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe told me about Valdemar while I tended the bar. An experiment between life and death! Finally, a case report with familiar working conditions.
host.teaser: A mesmerist attempts to hold a dying man at the boundary of life and death. Witnesses watch and wait. This clinical account becomes graphic; the grave is being asked to postpone an appointment.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we examine Poe’s unsettling Valdemar experiment?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Poe’s account, word for word. My memory remains beautifully preserved; no experimental procedure is required to keep the details together.
host.callback: Valdemar’s experiment gave us a grisly dispute over closing time. I admire a long stay, but even I would hesitate to advertise those preservation methods.
host.callbackShort: Valdemar’s case put the grave on a dreadful waiting list.

title: The Thing in the Hall
author: E. F. Benson
premise: Two men’s psychic experiments appear to produce something with an appetite of its own.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson brought this psychic experiment to my bar. Two men inviting unknown company! I do recommend checking the guest list before opening the door.
host.teaser: Two friends conduct psychic experiments and sense something answering them. Soon it seems capable of acting for itself. This particularly dark tale includes animal cruelty and gruesome deaths; the invitation has dreadful terms.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear about the thing in the hall?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Benson’s tale, word for word. My memory keeps the visitor securely on the page; this bar has quite enough spirits already.
host.callback: The thing in the hall gave us an appalling example of guest behavior. I adore company, but I draw a bony line at treating the household as a feeding arrangement.
host.callbackShort: That thing in the hall needed a grave lesson in manners.

title: The Pit and the Pendulum
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A prisoner must understand the terrible machinery and unseen hazards of a dark cell.

host.introduction: Edgar Allan Poe brought this prisoner’s tale to my bar. Such ingenious accommodations! I prefer a stool with fewer moving parts and no execution schedule.
host.teaser: A prisoner wakes in a dark cell and studies the hazards around him. Neither the floor nor the machinery overhead offers comfort. Time is becoming a particularly sharp concern.
host.offerQuestion: Shall we hear the prisoner’s struggle with those dreadful hazards?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, I'd love to hear it
host.bridge: Poe’s words, word for word. My memory never skips a second; my heart stopped keeping time long before this shift.
host.callback: The pit and pendulum gave us some magnificently dreadful suspense. I enjoy an evening that lingers; I simply prefer the clock to keep its hands to itself.
host.callbackShort: That prisoner had a terribly sharp appointment with time.

title: The Man Who Went Too Far
author: E. F. Benson
premise: A man’s pursuit of perfect communion with nature brings him close to something ancient.

host.introduction: E. F. Benson told me this tale of a man pursuing perfect joy. I grinned from ear to missing ear; happiness can have such interesting teeth.
host.teaser: A man seeks perfect happiness in nature by shutting out pain. A visiting friend finds him strangely changed. Something ancient may be taking an interest in this remarkably selective appreciation of the world.
host.offerQuestion: Would you like to hear where that pursuit of joy leads?
host.acceptLabel: Yes, tell me this tale.
host.bridge: Benson’s words, word for word. My memory has kept every leaf; I lost the bloom in my cheeks some centuries earlier.
host.callback: The man who went too far gave us a dreadful garden of delights. I welcome a little joy, though I prefer it to introduce its darker relatives before the party starts.
host.callbackShort: That search for perfect happiness wandered into some grave company.
